title: The Mu'tazilah
hookLine: the theologians who stepped aside, and kept thinking about justice
tomorrow: The trial of the created Qur'an

cards: A mosque in Basra, in Iraq. The teacher al-Hasan al-Basri sits with his students, and someone asks a hard question. A Muslim commits a grave sin.
Is he still a believer, or has he left the faith? Before the teacher can answer, a student, Wasil ibn Ata, offers a third answer: neither. A place in between.
Then he gets up, moves to another pillar, and some of the others go with him. That, at least, is the story people tell about how a group got its name: the Mu'tazilah, those who withdraw.

teach.h: REASON AS A GIFT, NOT A RIVAL.
teach.b: The Mu'tazilah were theologians who treated reason as a gift from Allah: a way to understand revelation, not a way around it.
They're remembered as calling themselves the people of justice and oneness. Justice first. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation, "Lo! Allah wrongeth not even of the weight of an ant."
The Mu'tazilah took that line all the way. If Allah is just, they argued, He does not punish people for what they could not help, so human beings must truly choose their own acts.
Reward and punishment only make sense if the choice is really ours. Then oneness.

They guarded tawhid so closely that they grew wary of anything eternal standing beside Allah. That led to the claim they're remembered for: the Qur'an is Allah's speech, and it was created, brought into being by Him.
To their ears, an uncreated Qur'an sounded like a second eternal thing next to God.

Their opponents heard it the other way around: the Qur'an is Allah's own speech, and His speech is not a made thing like a chair or a mountain. That disagreement didn't stay in the classroom; tomorrow it becomes a trial.

But the Mu'tazili question doesn't age. If God is just, what does that say about my choices? Later theologians, Sunni and Shia, answered it in different ways, and we'll meet some of them in this part.
The question, sharpened in Basra, is still on the table.

how: Students of Islamic theology study the Mu'tazilah as an early school of kalam that stressed Allah's justice and oneness, held that humans truly choose their acts, and taught that the Qur'an was created.

p: Allah wrongs no one, so choice is real

games.q: you're a student in Basra. someone asks: is a Muslim who commits a grave sin still a believer? what do you say?
games.why: in the story people tell, Wasil ibn Ata gave the third answer, then moved to another pillar, and the group got its name: those who withdraw.

practice: Bring to mind one small unfairness from this week, something you saw or something you did, and don't solve it or judge anyone. Just ask quietly: what would a just response look like here?
If you pray, you can recall the line, Allah wrongeth not even of the weight of an ant; if you don't, the plain question is enough.

carryVoice: Your line: justice and reason. A just God, and choices that are really ours. See you tomorrow.
